body:
**Note that this does not just change the behavior when using a custom IEqualityComparer**, as XUnit is [internally using equality comparers](https://github.com/xunit/assert.xunit/blob/1886f12618ad509776fd977cdcffbc772a4957c2/EqualityAsserts.cs#L81) in the overload without equality comparers.

For example we have a case in our code where an `Assert.Equal(x, y)` suddenly fails with two strings. Looking at the details the two strings are different but equivalent under unicode rules (i.e. `StringComparison.InvariantCulture` will treat the strings as equal). Up to now this assert succeeded; after updating XUnit it fails.

This looks like a serious regression to me.

~@Kharos I can't get your repro to compile, because I'm missing the `ToBitString` function.~

Never mind, I was able to guess what the implementation was well enough to verify the bug.
That doesn't call `Assert.Equal<T>`, it calls the special string overload.
Out of curiosity, why are you bypassing the built-in string comparison? It's much more useful. Is it because it makes this case pass?
This is still broken in 2.5.1-pre.9, and I'm not sure I know enough about what you're trying to accomplish here to understand why it's broken or how to fix it. Either way, please open a new issue.

> Out of curiosity, why are you bypassing the built-in string comparison? It's much more useful. Is it because it makes this case pass?

I am not the original author of that test case so I have to give my best guess. Reading the code it passes some json into a wrapped json parser and then compares the property value that is coming out to the expected property value. As json properties are not necessarily strings, the signature of the C# property that holds the parsed json value ends up `object`.

It also has different output results, depending on the runner, but I suspect that's because `dotnet test` does not set its console output format to Unicode (our console runner sets the console output to UTF-8):

![image](https://github.com/xunit/xunit/assets/16944/63ca7390-7c77-4f54-8fe8-ee56d0c8b290)

.NET 7 doesn't think they're equal:

![image](https://github.com/xunit/xunit/assets/16944/cbba992e-7484-4e93-bdda-d665d840eb02)

Honestly at the moment I'm leaning towards this being an "accidental & unintended feature" in 2.4.x.

> It also has different output results, depending on the runner

Both of these are ok, our original Jenkins output was:
```
Expected: ééé
Actual:   ééé
```
You can imagine the confusion that this caused 😂.

> Either way, please open a new issue.

I am still debating with myself if I should. On the one hand I feel like the new behavior is "more correct" as the two strings are not equal (and the `Assert.Equal<string>` overload will fail this case). On the other hand it is an undocumented behavior change...

> On the other hand it is an undocumented behavior change...

I have no problem with saying that unintended behavior is unsupported. I've done it more than once in the past when closing issues. It's impossible to cover every single case when so many of them are simply unknown ahead of time (like this one). I have a bit of curiosity as to exactly _why_ it passed in the past, but that doesn't necessarily mean I want to revert to the old behavior. When in doubt, behaving like the framework does (unless we're explicitly and purposefully doing something different) is a pretty good rule of thumb for me.

Another data point, for what it's worth: Powershell's `-eq` operator considers the strings to be equal:

![image](https://github.com/xunit/xunit/assets/16944/2825e82f-b5dc-4cc1-bd95-906b793b10de)
